newsitem.title: USA: April US durable goods orders look slightly weaker.
newsitem.headline: April US durable goods orders look slightly weaker.

text.p: U.S. durable goods orders rose 1.4 percent in April but economists said a decline in unfilled orders and a subdued trend in orders for non-defense capital goods gave a weaker cast to the report.

The government reported that U.S. durable goods orders rose 1.4 percent in April after a revised 2.2 percent drop in March. Economists polled by Reuters had offered an average forecast of a 1.3 percent rise in April orders. March orders were originally reported as having fallen 2.6 percent.
Defense goods orders, which fluctuate sharply from month to month, soared 28.0 percent in April, Commerce Department said.

"(There were) a lot of defense orders in (April's report) and so perhaps, underneath the surface, you have some small sense of weakening here," said Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co International.
Brusca noted that without transportation orders, another volatile item, April orders were up just 0.5 percent after a 1.7 percent drop in March.
Brusca called the report a reasonable one that seemed to fit with other recent reports on the economy.
"The industrial production numbers were flat in April so seeing slightly weaker durable goods numbers is not a big surprise," he said.
Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said U.S. Treasury prices rose in reaction to the durable goods data because they were weaker than some had feared.
"There wasn't as much of a bounceback from the 2.2 percent drop in March as one might have anticipated," said Schaja.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond, down 1/8 of a point before the report, erased that loss and rose another 1/8 of a point after it.
Economists had thought that auto industry strikes during April might depress transportation orders. But transportation equipment orders rose 4.5 percent.
"They might have been up even more were it not for the strike," said Schaja.
Two consecutive months of declines in unfilled orders provided another hint of weakness in the durable goods orders picture, economists said.
Total unfilled orders fell 0.4 percent in April and a revised 0.4 percent in March after a 0.7 percent rise in February.

"After a long period of rising levels of unfilled orders, we're seeing unfilled orders levels come down," said Alan Ruskin, chief economist at I.D.E.A. "That's probably a constructive sign as far as relieving potential bottlenecks in the economy that could create inflation.

In conjunction with the NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management) index's May supplier delivery time reading of 53.4 -- a contrast to the peak reading in that series of 65.7 in 1994 during the last monetary policy tightening cycle -- the declines in unfilled orders for durable goods is "encouraging," said Ruskin.
